One thing she wanted to do, however, was me not seeing her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed. She kept saying I’d love it, she loved it. She and her best friend (maid of honor) kept sharing reaction posts of grooms happy crying upon getting a first look at their bride, tagging me in it, saying “this will be you!” Day of, wife walks down. She herself did look beautiful, as always. However, I was not big on the dress. To me, it wasn’t at all flattering. But I didn’t focus on that. I focused on her. I smiled. I said I was estatic to marry her and that showed, without me being over dramatic. I also said I had her friend nudging me the whole time and that was unfair to me. Finally I asked if we had a wedding or a play, because I never got lines. Now she’s mad at me. Am I an ass here? I do feel bad she’s disappointed but I couldn’t force myself to have a reaction.

The experience of fasting from dawn to sunset for an entire month can be transformative, and it's not uncommon for individuals to report changes in their perspective and values as a result. Research has shown that experiences like Ramadan can lead to increased empathy, self-awareness, and a greater appreciation for the struggles of others. The physical and emotional challenges of fasting can foster a sense of gratitude, humility, and compassion, which can, in turn, influence what people value most in life. Here are some possible ways that living through Ramadan might shape one's values: 1. **Appreciation for simplicity and gratitude**: The experience of fasting can help individuals appreciate the simple things in life, like food, water, and relationships. This can lead to a greater sense of gratitude and contentment. 2. **Empathy and compassion**: By experiencing hunger and thirst, individuals may develop a deeper understanding of the struggles of those who face food insecurity or other forms of hardship. This can foster empathy and a desire to help others. 3. **Prioritization of relationships**: The communal aspect of Ramadan, where families and friends come together to break their fasts, can strengthen social bonds and emphasize the importance of relationships. 4. **Spiritual growth and self-reflection**: The introspective nature of Ramadan can lead to a greater focus on one's spiritual growth, self-awareness, and personal development. 5. **Appreciation for the value of time**: The experience of fasting can help individuals appreciate the value of time and make the most of the time they have with loved ones. 6. **Resilience and self-discipline**: The physical and emotional challenges of fasting can build resilience and self-discipline, which can translate to other areas of life. 7. **Community and belonging**: The shared experience of Ramadan can create a sense of community and belonging, which can be a powerful source of motivation and support. It's essential to note that these changes in values and priorities can be highly individualized and may vary from person to person. Some people may experience a more profound shift in their values, while others may not notice significant changes. In your case, living through Ramadan every year can indeed shape your values and priorities. AITA for not being emotional on my wedding day? | My wife and I didn’t do many traditional things for our wedding. One thing she wanted to do, however, was me not seeing her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed. She kept saying I’d love it, she loved it. She and her best friend (maid of honor) kept sharing reaction posts of grooms happy crying upon getting a first look at their bride, tagging me in it, saying “this will be you!” Day of, wife walks down. She herself did look beautiful, as always. However, I was not big on the dress. To me, it wasn’t at all flattering. But I didn’t focus on that. I focused on her. I smiled. I didn’t break down in tears like some reaction pics/videos. The maid of honor kept nudging me until I looked at her and mouthed “stop”. We got married, kissed, the whole thing. Everything was fine at the reception. Then after our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend and asked why I had an “underwhelming” reaction to her coming down the aisle. I said I didn’t. She said there are pictures that guests took and I don’t look how she pictured. I asked if she wanted me to cry and she said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I said I was estatic to marry her and that showed, without me being over dramatic. I also said I had her friend nudging me the whole time and that was unfair to me. Finally I asked if we had a wedding or a play, because I never got lines. Now she’s mad at me. Am I an ass here? I do feel bad she’s disappointed but I couldn’t force myself to have a reaction.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: A classic Reddit "Am I The Asshole?" (AITA) scenario! After reading the story, I'd say: **NTA (Not The Asshole)** Here's why: 1. **You agreed to the surprise**: You knew your wife wanted to keep the dress a secret, and you agreed to it. You didn't promise to have a specific emotional reaction. 2. **You focused on her, not the dress**: You chose to smile and enjoy the moment, rather than getting caught up in your initial disappointment with the dress. That shows you were present and appreciative of the occasion. 3. **You didn't mislead her**: You didn't pretend to be more emotional than you felt. You simply didn't have the reaction she expected, but you still expressed your happiness and love for her. 4. **You stood up for yourself**: When her friend kept nudging you, you politely asked her to stop. That's a reasonable boundary to set, especially on your wedding day. 5. **You didn't try to manipulate her expectations**: You didn't try to make her feel better by faking a reaction. You simply explained your feelings and perspective. It's understandable that your wife might have been disappointed by your reaction, but it's not unreasonable to expect you to have a specific emotional response. You did, however, express your happiness and love for her, which is what truly matters. In the end, it's not about meeting someone's expectations of how you should react; it's about being true to yourself and enjoying the moment. You did that, and that's something to be proud of.
